title: The letters round: nine random letters, one long word

body.heading: How the round works
paragraphs: Write the alphabet on slips of paper, keeping vowels (A, E, I, O, U) in one pile and consonants in another. Draw three or four vowels and five or six consonants, lay out your nine letters, and set a timer for sixty seconds. Everyone writes down the longest word they can build, using each letter at most as many times as it appears.
When time is up, read your words aloud from shortest to longest for maximum drama. Score one point per letter in your best word — and double points, by house tradition, for anyone who uses all nine.

body.heading: Tricks the regulars use
paragraphs: Hunt for endings first. If you can spot -ING, -ED, -ER or -TION among your letters, you only need a short stem to reach a long word. Common pairs help too: QU, CH, SH and TH often unlock words that the raw letters seemed to forbid.

Do not fall in love with your first word. A six-letter find in the first ten seconds is a safety net, not a finish line — keep scanning for the seven hiding behind it. Many a round is won by the player who kept shuffling while others relaxed.

body.heading: Try it: tonight's edition
paragraphs: Play three rounds and keep a running total. To level the field between strong spellers and beginners, let younger players score double for any word of five letters or more, or give everyone the option of swapping one letter between rounds.
Keep a family record book of the best words ever found from nine letters. It becomes a small hall of fame — and a standing invitation for somebody to beat the nine-letter legend at the top.

takeaway: Nine letters, sixty seconds, one long word: the letters round proves a game show can fit inside an envelope of paper slips.
